source.authors: Anderson JM, Clegg TM, Véras LVMVQ, Holland KN
source.title: Insight into shark magnetic field perception from empirical observations

value: 100% conditioned response in all unimpaired sharks (group-level counts) to every applied field intensity, 0.03 to 2.89 microtesla; the authors cannot rule out an electrosensory response to induced electric transients
method: behavioural: conditioned approach to a food target during a coil-generated magnetic stimulus; intensities used in training and conditioning
conditions: Captive sandbar sharks in a 7 m diameter circular tank, conditioned with a food reward to seek a target when a magnetic stimulus (coil of 18 AWG copper wire around the tank) was on; stimulus intensities 0.03 to 2.89 microtesla; unimpaired series 10 trials with 5 sharks in the first eight and 7 in the last two
quote: Unimpaired, conditioned sharks produced a 100% response (all sharks demonstrating a conditioned response) to all applied magnetic field intensities used in training and conditioning, which ranged from 0.03 to 2.89 micro-Tesla (μT).
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0; full text read on the publisher's own free copy (link.springer.com, Scientific Reports). Name: ACCEPTED, exact match in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv (GBIF usage key 2418009). 0.03 microtesla was the weakest field applied, so the sentence gives no detection limit below it. Confound: the authors calculate that at 0.029 µT the maximum induced transient voltage gradient was 74.35 nV cm/s−1 at the tank periphery and that it 'remained above the 30 nV cm−1 median sensory threshold across more than half of the experimental arena' (Results, Electrical field measurement and calculation); the Discussion states 'Thus, we cannot definitively rule out the shark electrosense being involved in observed conditioned responses.' Counts were pooled across sharks because individuals could not be reliably identified (Materials and Methods, Data Collection and Analysis), so 'all sharks' is a group-level statement.

source.authors: Desai R, Garratt MA, Srinivasan MV, Ravi S
source.title: Effects of object motion on visual acuity in honeybees

value: stationary targets: Abstract says shape change (disc vs diamond) perceived only above 1.9 degrees, but the Results show significant discrimination at 1.9 degrees (68%, p = 0.0232) and 3.1 degrees, none at 0.88 or 0.44 degrees; stationary threshold between 0.88 and 1.9 degrees
method: behavioural: Y-maze choice after training, stationary disc against diamond at four sizes
conditions: Y-maze binary choice: foragers trained to a stimulus on a sugar-solution feeder, then tested with empty nectaries; stimuli (disc vs diamond) 3D-printed from one PETG filament spool; sizes 3.1, 1.9, 0.88 and 0.44 degrees; N = 50 bees per size (five sets of 10); moving stimuli oscillated side to side at +/-20 degrees and 3.5 Hz; viewing distance not stated; no contrast or brightness measurements reported
quote: When stimuli were stationary, bees perceived the change in shape only for targets that subtended visual angles >1.9°.
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0 (licence from 2026-04-22; issue date 2026-04-15); full text read on the publisher's own free PDF (journals.biologists.com). Name: ACCEPTED in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. The Abstract says '>1.9°', but the Results table gives significant discrimination at 1.9 degrees (chi-squared p = 0.0232, binomial p = 0.0153) as well as 3.1 degrees (p = 0.0007; 0.0003) and none at 0.88 degrees (p = 0.1491; 0.1189) or 0.44 degrees (p = 0.3818; 0.1611), so the stationary threshold lies between 0.88 and 1.9 degrees on the Results. The authors report angular size, not cycles per degree, so no acuity_cpd is computed.

source.authors: Desai R, Garratt MA, Srinivasan MV, Ravi S
source.title: Effects of object motion on visual acuity in honeybees

value: moving stimulus preferred over a stationary one at every size tested, down to 0.44 degrees
method: behavioural: Y-maze choice, stationary against moving stimulus
conditions: Y-maze binary choice: foragers trained to a stimulus on a sugar-solution feeder, then tested with empty nectaries; this test: moving disc against stationary disc, bees trained only to the stationary disc; stimuli (disc vs diamond) 3D-printed from one PETG filament spool; sizes 3.1, 1.9, 0.88 and 0.44 degrees; N = 50 bees per size (five sets of 10); moving stimuli oscillated side to side at +/-20 degrees and 3.5 Hz; viewing distance not stated; no contrast or brightness measurements reported
quote: However, when presented with a stationary and a moving stimulus, they consistently preferred the moving stimulus, even when both stimuli subtended angles as small as 0.44°.
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0 (licence from 2026-04-22; issue date 2026-04-15); full text read on the publisher's own free PDF (journals.biologists.com). Name: ACCEPTED in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. The authors also report that motion cues override a learned preference for a familiar stationary shape (Abstract). Motion was produced by servo-driven oscillation; the Discussion gives peak angular velocities up to 500 deg/s and averages near 350 deg/s. Stimuli were shape-matched in material but contrast and brightness were not measured, so a luminance-flicker cue from the moving target cannot be excluded.

source.authors: Desai R, Garratt MA, Srinivasan MV, Ravi S
source.title: Effects of object motion on visual acuity in honeybees

value: disc and diamond discriminated at 0.44 degrees when both targets moved, not when both were stationary
method: behavioural: Y-maze choice, shape discrimination with both targets moving against both stationary
conditions: Y-maze binary choice: foragers trained to a stimulus on a sugar-solution feeder, then tested with empty nectaries; stimuli (disc vs diamond) 3D-printed from one PETG filament spool; sizes 3.1, 1.9, 0.88 and 0.44 degrees; N = 50 bees per size (five sets of 10); moving stimuli oscillated side to side at +/-20 degrees and 3.5 Hz; viewing distance not stated; no contrast or brightness measurements reported
quote: Most notably, bees successfully discriminated shapes at the smallest tested size of 0.44° when both targets were in motion, but not when they were stationary.
note: Licence: Crossref vor CC BY 4.0 (licence from 2026-04-22; issue date 2026-04-15); full text read on the publisher's own free PDF (journals.biologists.com). Name: ACCEPTED in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. Results: with both targets moving, the trained diamond was preferred 70% at 3.1 degrees and 72% at 0.44 degrees (N = 50 per size). The paper concludes that motion enhances acuity beyond earlier stationary-target limits; it tests only 0.44 degrees as the smallest size, so the lower bound for moving targets is not found. Experiment 4 tested only 0.44 and 3.1 degrees; the stationary comparison is Experiment 1 (other bees). The paper's Experiment 4 statistics at 3.1 degrees repeat Experiment 3's at 0.44 degrees, a likely copying error that does not affect the 0.44-degree value. The moving target oscillates ±20 degrees, so this is shape discrimination of a moving target, not a static acuity.
